title: April minutes show support for two-sided guidance extended well beyond three formal dissents
summary: The 28–29 April meeting produced three different answers to the question of how divided the Fed was. Eleven of twelve voters wanted to keep the federal funds target at 3.50–3.75%. Nine accepted the language governing possible future adjustments. Eight voted for the entire package. Stephen Miran wanted an immediate quarter-point cut. Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan supported the hold but rejected what they saw as an easing bias. The minutes released on 20 May added an important fact about the wider group of participants, which includes nonvoters. Many would have removed the directional language, and a majority thought some tightening would likely be appropriate if inflation persisted above 2%. The difference between eight votes for the statement and eleven for the rate measures a disagreement about guidance. The majority discussing a conditional hike gives a sense of how quickly the debate could change if the inflation forecast disappointed.

The inflation evidence available to the meeting had clearly deteriorated. The staff's economic review put February headline and core PCE inflation at 2.8% and 3.0%. Using already available producer and consumer prices, staff estimated that March readings would be 3.5% and 3.2%. The March numbers were estimates, not yet observations on the same footing as February. Higher fuel costs accounted for much of the headline acceleration and affected shipping and airfares. Other disruptions raised fertiliser prices. Participants also reported continuing tariff effects on goods and new price pressure in information technology. A few observed that software prices could contribute appreciably to measured core inflation while providing relatively little information about where aggregate inflation would go next. A core measure could therefore move further from target even while housing services continued to disinflate.

The staff forecast and the participants' risk discussion addressed different horizons. Staff raised its inflation projection for the current year but still expected disinflation after the first half, with inflation close to 2% at the end of 2027. That baseline required conflict-related effects to diminish and earlier tariff increases to work through prices. Almost all participants considered a scenario in which disruption persisted, or commodity prices stayed high after fighting ended. Several asked whether repeated shocks after years of above-target inflation would begin to change wage and price setting. Several also saw scope for productivity gains to reduce pressure. Most judged longer-term inflation expectations stable. That observation is compatible with a serious risk of future deterioration. It does not require the Committee to conclude that expectations had already shifted.

Activity and hiring complicate the case for acting on inflation immediately. First-quarter GDP appeared to rebound partly because the federal shutdown ended. Rising imports of high-tech goods dragged on net exports even as expenditure on technology supported domestic investment. Staff therefore also examined real private domestic final purchases, comprising household consumption and private fixed investment. They appeared to grow a little faster than their average pace in the preceding year. March unemployment was 4.3%. Payrolls rebounded after the temporary effects of a health-care strike and harsh February weather, but average job gains remained low. Annual hourly earnings growth was 3.5%, seven-tenths less than a year earlier. Faster payroll growth in one month and slower wage growth over a year each measured something quite different from an ongoing increase in labour demand.

The staff nudged up its activity forecast. Supportive financing, investment related to artificial intelligence and an eventual fading of other headwinds would allow output to grow slightly faster than potential in coming years. Many participants judged employment stable, while most continued to see its risks as tilted downwards. A low-hiring economy can have little spare employment demand to absorb displaced workers. Some participants saw low hiring as proportionate to slower labour supply. Others cited concentrated payroll gains and weaker survey measures of job availability. Energy costs could also affect households unevenly. Participants reported strain among lower-income households and at farms buying fuel and fertiliser, even as wealth and fiscal support sustained aggregate consumption. These observations help explain how both future restraint and future easing could remain plausible under the same current rate.

The New York Fed trading desk described a pre-meeting oil futures curve above March's but still steeply downward sloping. The manager warned that the curve had a mixed forecasting record. Surveyed near-term inflation expectations rose again, while expectations for 2027 and beyond changed little. In interest-rate options the probability of a hike by the first quarter of 2027 was about 30%. In the Desk survey the median of respondents' most likely paths still featured two quarter-point cuts over the coming year, now expected later. The survey summarises a most likely path, while options price a distribution and compensation for uncertainty. Those readings can differ even before allowing for different people supplying each observation. Neither tells us what investors learnt upon publication of the minutes.

The Treasury curve also resists a single interpretation. A model reported by the manager attributed much of the rise in the two-year nominal yield since the conflict began to expected inflation, partly offset by a decline in the expected real rate. At ten years, the estimated inflation revision was smaller and risk premia rose. These components were model estimates. Liquidity remained favourable despite periods of greater volatility. Equity markets recovered as earnings expectations strengthened and geopolitical tensions eased, and corporate spreads narrowed. Credit access nevertheless remained relatively difficult for small businesses and weaker mortgage borrowers. Corporate issuance included speculative-grade borrowing for AI capital expenditure, while private credit loan issuance slowed. Some software borrowers used payment-in-kind to defer interest. A tight public bond spread and a low recorded default rate could thus coexist with pressure on cash flow outside public credit markets.

April's tax date supplied a concrete test of the operating framework. Tax receipts raised Treasury's account balance and sharply reduced reserves. The drop was close to the Desk's expectations. Effective federal funds remained one basis point below interest on reserve balances, while secured funding rates rose only modestly around 15 April. Excluding transactions required to maintain eligibility, that date accounted for the period's standing repo usage. The manager saw the willingness to borrow even when interdealer rates were only a little above the facility rate as evidence of more routine usage. The Committee also completed the scheduled annual renewal of existing international liquidity swap arrangements. A large reserve decline, take-up of a standing facility and a renewed backstop therefore have distinct meanings. The minutes tie the first to tax flows, the second to the economics of funding, and the third to an annual decision. None constitutes an additional change in the target rate.

For an event study, 29 April and 20 May are different information dates. The decision and named dissenters were already public after the meeting. The potentially informative addition in May was how widespread the discomfort with an easing bias had been and which conditions might justify a cut or a hike. The market review documents repricing before the meeting, during a period that also included a cease-fire, earnings news and supply disruption. It cannot establish the response of markets to the later publication.

questions.question: Did publishing the breadth of support for removing the easing bias change the expected rate path?
questions.detail: Recover rate probabilities immediately before and after 20 May and compare contracts spanning the rest of 2026 with options extending to early 2027. Control for information released after the April decision, including already public explanations from the three guidance dissenters. A shift in upside probabilities need not be accompanied by a comparable change in the most likely rate.

questions.question: Would energy pass-through raise the underlying inflation trend after the initial commodity price shock?
questions.detail: Separate freight and airfares from housing, technology and other services; compare changes in costs, selling prices and margins at firms with different exposures. Look for repeated repricing and evidence that wage settlements or longer-term expectations respond. A temporary jump in one high-weight software category could move the core index without supporting that conclusion.

questions.question: Did domestic demand remain firm while financing tightened for borrowers least able to substitute funding?
questions.detail: Compare final private purchases with investment by industry and with consumption across household income groups. Follow public bond issuance, private loan flows, cash versus deferred interest payments and credit terms for small firms. An apparently easy aggregate credit environment could conceal a meaningful restriction for borrowers reliant on private lenders.

questions.question: Was April's orderly tax settlement evidence of ample liquidity across institutions?
questions.detail: Measure reserves, secured rates, transaction dispersion, and standing repo take-up on and around 15 April. Compare with quarter-end and other settlement dates, accounting for the Treasury account balance and reserve-management purchases. Stable average rates would provide stronger evidence if institutions generally retained access to funding at similar terms.
